s3-bio-01.stem: A researcher used elemental analysis to determine the composition of three purified samples extracted from cultured cells. The results are shown in the table. Which statement correctly describes a characteristic of the data in the table?

stimulus.description: Table of elemental composition (percent of dry mass) of three purified biological samples for C, H, O, N, P, S.

data.title: Elemental composition of three purified samples

options.text: Nitrogen is found in two samples, but phosphorus is found in only one of them.
options.why: Correct: N is nonzero in samples 2 and 3 only, and P is nonzero only in sample 3.

options.text: Carbon makes up the greatest percentage of dry mass in every one of the samples.
options.why: Misconception: assuming carbon is always the most abundant element by mass because it is the backbone of organic molecules; in sample 1 oxygen (49.8) exceeds carbon (44.0).

options.text: Sample 1 has a higher percentage of hydrogen than either of the other samples.
options.why: Misconception: misreading the table columns or assuming carbohydrate-like samples are hydrogen-richest; sample 2 has the highest H (7.0 vs 6.2 and 4.4).

options.text: Sulfur is present in every sample that also contains a measurable amount of nitrogen.
options.why: Misconception: assuming N and S always occur together, as in proteins; sample 3 has N (15.0) but S is 0.0.

s3-bio-01.explanation_en: Reading the N and P columns: nitrogen is nonzero in two samples (2 and 3) while phosphorus is nonzero only in one (3), so the key is correct. Carbon is not the largest percentage in the sample with 49.8% oxygen versus 44.0% carbon, so the carbon-greatest statement is wrong. Hydrogen is highest in the sample with 7.0%, not in the sample with 6.2%, so the hydrogen statement is wrong. One sample contains nitrogen (15.0%) but no sulfur, so the sulfur-with-nitrogen statement is wrong.

s3-bio-02.stem: A student incubates three glucose polymers with amylase and tests for reducing sugars, with the results shown. Which statement best describes the structural basis for the difference between cellulose and the other two polysaccharides?

stimulus.description: Benedict's test results (reducing sugar) for three polysaccharide solutions before and after incubation with amylase for 30 minutes at 37 C.

data.notes: All three polysaccharides are polymers of glucose. A positive Benedict's test indicates free reducing sugar (monosaccharide or small sugar) is present.

options.text: Cellulose contains a different monomer than starch and glycogen, so amylase has no glucose-based substrate to hydrolyze in the cellulose solution.
options.why: Misconception: thinking cellulose is made of a different monomer; all three are glucose polymers, as the table note states.

options.text: Amylase hydrolyzes the alpha glycosidic linkages in starch and glycogen, but the beta linkages between glucose monomers in cellulose give a different shape the enzyme's active site cannot bind.
options.why: Correct: the alpha vs. beta glycosidic linkage changes the polymer shape, and the enzyme's active site is specific, so only alpha linkages are hydrolyzed, releasing reducing sugar.

options.text: Cellulose is too heavily branched for amylase to reach its linkages, whereas starch and glycogen are unbranched and fully exposed.
options.why: Misconception: reversing branching; cellulose is unbranched, while glycogen is highly branched and starch partly branched, yet both are digested.

options.text: Amylase forms new glycosidic bonds in starch and glycogen by dehydration synthesis, which produces the reducing sugar detected.
options.why: Misconception: confusing hydrolysis with dehydration synthesis; amylase breaks bonds by adding water, it does not build polymers.

s3-bio-02.explanation_en: All three substrates are glucose polymers and all test negative at the start, so none contains free reducing sugar. After amylase, starch and glycogen test positive because amylase hydrolyzes their alpha glycosidic linkages and releases glucose and small sugars. Cellulose stays negative because its beta linkages give a different, straight-chain shape that does not fit the enzyme's active site. The different-monomer option is wrong because all three are glucose polymers. The branching option is wrong because cellulose is unbranched and glycogen is highly branched, yet glycogen is digested. The bond-formation option is wrong because amylase uses hydrolysis, which breaks bonds, and dehydration synthesis would not release reducing sugar.

s3-bio-03.stem: A student analyzes the base composition of two purified nucleic acid samples and records the data shown in the table. Which statement best describes a characteristic of the data that supports an identification of the samples?

stimulus.description: Table of base composition (mole percent) for two purified nucleic acid samples, X and Y, from a lab analysis.

data.title: Base composition of two purified nucleic acid samples
data.units: mole percent of total bases; each row sums to 100

options.text: Sample X is likely double-stranded DNA, because it has no uracil; sample Y is likely double-stranded RNA, because its adenine and uracil totals differ from guanine and cytosine.
options.why: Misconception: calls Y double-stranded RNA; in double-stranded RNA A would equal U and G would equal C, but Y has A 31 vs U 26 and G 24 vs C 19, so it is not double-stranded.

options.text: Sample X is likely RNA, because its adenine equals thymine and its guanine equals cytosine; sample Y is likely DNA, because its bases do not pair equally.
options.why: Misconception: thinks equal base percentages indicate RNA and unequal indicate DNA; ignores that thymine marks DNA and uracil marks RNA.

options.text: Sample X is likely double-stranded DNA, because its adenine equals thymine and its guanine equals cytosine; sample Y is likely RNA, because it contains uracil.
options.why: Correct: X has A=T (22=22) and G=C (28=28), the base-pairing equivalence of double-stranded DNA with thymine and no uracil; Y has uracil and no thymine, so it is RNA.

options.text: Sample X and sample Y are both likely DNA, because each contains adenine, guanine, and cytosine in different amounts.
options.why: Misconception: ignores thymine/uracil difference; thinks presence of A, G, C alone identifies DNA, though Y contains uracil instead of thymine.

s3-bio-03.explanation_en: Sample X has adenine equal to thymine (22 each) and guanine equal to cytosine (28 each), the complementary-pairing pattern of double-stranded DNA, and it has thymine but no uracil. Sample Y has uracil and no thymine, so it is RNA, and its unequal values (A 31 vs U 26, G 24 vs C 19) indicate it is single-stranded. The option calling X RNA reverses the roles of thymine and equal pairing percentages. The option calling Y double-stranded RNA fails because a double-stranded molecule would show A=U and G=C, which the data do not. The option calling both DNA ignores that Y has uracil and no thymine.

s3-bio-04.stem: The table shows the base composition of four purified nucleic acid samples. Based on the patterns in the table, which sample is most likely double-stranded DNA?

stimulus.description: Table of base composition (mole percent) for four purified nucleic acid samples.

data.title: Base composition of four purified nucleic acid samples
data.units: mole percent of total bases; each row sums to 100

options.text: Sample 4, because adenine equals thymine and uracil is present in a small amount
options.why: Misconception: notes A=T but ignores that uracil is found in RNA, not DNA, and that G (20) does not equal C (10).

options.text: Sample 2, because adenine equals cytosine and guanine exceeds uracil
options.why: Misconception: treats any matching percentages as pairing evidence; this sample has uracil and no thymine (RNA), and A pairs with U/T, not C.

options.text: Sample 3, because it contains thymine and has more purines than pyrimidines
options.why: Misconception: thinks presence of thymine alone proves double-stranded DNA; A (20) does not equal T (25) and G (35) does not equal C (20), so it is likely single-stranded DNA.

options.text: Sample 1, because adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine
options.why: Correct: A=T (22=22) and G=C (28=28) with no uracil, which is the base-pairing pattern of double-stranded DNA.

s3-bio-04.explanation_en: Double-stranded DNA pairs A with T and G with C, so the amounts of A and T match, the amounts of G and C match, and uracil is absent. The sample with A=22, T=22, G=28, C=28 and no uracil fits this. The sample with uracil and no thymine is RNA, and its A=25 pairs with U=20 do not match, so it is not paired DNA. The sample with thymine but A=20, T=25, G=35, C=20 lacks the A=T and G=C equalities, so it is likely single-stranded DNA; having thymine and extra purines does not show double strandedness. The sample with both thymine and uracil and unequal G and C fits neither DNA nor RNA pairing.

s3-bio-05.stem: A student uses the agar cubes in the table as models of cells of different sizes. The student wants to graph the surface-area-to-volume ratio (y-axis) against side length (x-axis, 0 to 8 mm). Which description best represents the relationship shown by these data?

stimulus.description: Table of cube side length, surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio for four agar cubes used as cell models.

data.title: Agar cube cell models

options.text: A horizontal line, because surface area and volume both increase as side length increases, so the ratio stays constant
options.why: Misconception: assuming that because both quantities increase, their ratio stays the same; volume increases faster (cubed) than surface area (squared).

options.text: A straight line that falls by the same amount for each 1 mm increase in side length, reaching zero at 8 mm
options.why: Misconception: assuming a linear relationship; the data show unequal drops (6 to 3 is a drop of 3 over 1 mm, 3 to 1.5 is 1.5 over 2 mm) and the ratio never reaches zero.

options.text: A curve that rises as side length increases, because larger cubes have more surface area available for exchange
options.why: Misconception: confusing total surface area with the ratio; surface area rises but volume rises faster, so the ratio falls.

options.text: A curve that falls steeply from 1 mm to 2 mm and then flattens, with the ratio halving each time side length doubles
options.why: Correct: ratio = 6/s, so it falls from 6 to 3 to 1.5 to 0.75, halving with each doubling, giving a decreasing curve that levels off.

s3-bio-05.explanation_en: The ratio equals 6/side length: 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75 mm^-1 for sides of 1, 2, 4, 8 mm. Each doubling of side length halves the ratio, so a graph would be a decreasing curve that is steep at small sizes and flattens at larger sizes. The straight-line option is wrong because the decreases are not constant per mm and the ratio never reaches zero. The rising-curve option confuses total surface area, which does increase, with the ratio, which decreases because volume grows faster than surface area. The horizontal-line option is wrong because volume scales with the cube of side length while surface area scales with its square, so the ratio is not constant.

s3-bio-06.stem: A catering business compares cube-shaped boxes of different sizes to model how cell size affects exchange of materials across the cell surface. Using the table, the owner plots surface area-to-volume ratio (cm^2/cm^3, y-axis) against side length (cm, x-axis). Which description best represents the relationship the plot should show and its biological meaning?

stimulus.description: Table of cube side length, surface area, volume for four cube-shaped insulated delivery boxes used as a model of cells.

options.text: A straight line that rises, because surface area increases as side length increases, so larger cells exchange materials more efficiently
options.why: Confuses total surface area with the ratio; the ratio actually decreases as size increases.

options.text: A curve that falls steeply and then levels off, because the ratio equals 6 divided by side length, so larger cells have less surface per unit of volume for exchange
options.why: Correct: ratio = 6/s gives 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75, a decreasing, leveling curve; larger size means less surface per volume.

options.text: A straight line that falls by the same amount for each doubling of side length, because volume and surface area change by equal amounts, so cell size does not affect exchange
options.why: Assumes a linear decrease; the ratio halves with each doubling (not constant drops of 3, 1.5, 0.75), and surface area and volume do not change by equal amounts.

options.text: A horizontal line, because every cube has the same shape, so the ratio of surface area to volume stays constant as cells grow
options.why: Assumes the same shape means the same ratio; ignores that volume grows faster (cubed) than surface area (squared).

s3-bio-06.explanation_en: The ratio of surface area to volume is 6, 3, 1.5, and 0.75 for sides of 1, 2, 4, and 8 cm, which fits 6 divided by side length. Plotting these gives a curve that falls steeply and then levels off, because volume (cubed) grows faster than surface area (squared). For cells, a larger size means less membrane per unit of volume for exchanging materials. The option claiming a rising line confuses total surface area with the ratio. The option claiming equal linear drops is wrong because the ratio halves with each doubling, so the drops shrink (3, then 1.5, then 0.75). The option claiming a horizontal line ignores that same shape does not mean the same ratio when size changes.

s3-bio-07.stem: A model treats cells as cubes. The table gives the surface area, volume, and surface-area-to-volume ratio (SA:V) for cubes of increasing side length. Which graph of SA:V (y-axis, units^-1) versus side length (x-axis, units) best represents the relationship shown in the table?

stimulus.description: Table of cube side length, surface area, volume, and surface-area-to-volume ratio for four cubes.

options.text: A curve that increases steeply at small side lengths and then flattens as side length increases
options.why: Misconception: believes bigger cells have more surface area relative to volume, ignoring that volume grows faster (s^3) than surface area (s^2).

options.text: A straight line that decreases at a constant rate, reaching zero at a side length of 8 units
options.why: Misconception: assumes a linear relationship; the drops (3, 1.5, 0.75 per doubling) are not constant, and the ratio is 0.75 at s = 8, not zero.

options.text: A curve that decreases steeply at small side lengths and then flattens, approaching but never reaching zero
options.why: Correct: SA:V = 6/s, a decreasing curve with halving each time s doubles; drops 6 to 3 (by 3) then 3 to 1.5 to 0.75, flattening and never reaching zero.

options.text: A horizontal line, because surface area and volume both increase as side length increases
options.why: Misconception: thinks that because both SA and V increase, their ratio is constant; the ratio actually changes because they scale at different rates.

s3-bio-07.explanation_en: SA grows with s squared while V grows with s cubed, so SA:V = 6/s. The table shows the ratio halving each time the side length doubles (6, 3, 1.5, 0.75), which gives a curve that falls steeply at first, then flattens and approaches zero without reaching it. The straight-line option is wrong because the decreases are not constant and the ratio at s = 8 is 0.75, not zero. The increasing-curve option reverses the trend in the data. The horizontal-line option ignores that volume increases faster than surface area, so the ratio is not constant.

s3-bio-08.stem: A biotech supply company sells liposomes that each contain a fixed number of glucose carrier proteins and is deciding whether to recommend that a customer run its assay in 80 mM glucose instead of 40 mM to speed up glucose uptake. Based on the data, which prediction about doubling the external glucose concentration from 40 mM to 80 mM is best supported?

stimulus.description: Glucose uptake rate by carrier-containing liposomes at six external glucose concentrations.

data.title: Glucose uptake by liposomes containing a glucose carrier protein (internal glucose kept near 0 mM)
data.conditions: Same temperature and same number of carriers per mg lipid in all trials; no ATP supplied.

options.text: Uptake will increase only slightly, because nearly all carriers are already occupied at 40 mM.
options.why: Correct: the rate plateaus (75 to 76 at the top), showing carrier saturation, so the rate is limited by the number of carriers.

options.text: Uptake will roughly double, because facilitated diffusion rate is proportional to the concentration gradient.
options.why: Misconception: treating facilitated diffusion like simple diffusion, with a rate that increases linearly with gradient without limit.

options.text: Uptake will decrease, because high glucose concentration denatures the carrier proteins.
options.why: Misconception: assuming high solute concentration damages proteins; the data show no decline between 40 and 80 mM.

options.text: Uptake will roughly double, because the cell will use ATP to pump in additional glucose at high concentration.
options.why: Misconception: thinking facilitated diffusion involves ATP-driven pumping; no ATP is supplied and the process is passive.

s3-bio-08.explanation_en: Uptake rises steeply at low concentrations but levels off (72, 75, 76 nmol/min per mg lipid at 20, 40, 80 mM), because the fixed number of carrier proteins becomes saturated. Doubling from 40 to 80 mM therefore raises the rate by only about 1%. The prediction of a doubling treats facilitated diffusion as unlimited simple diffusion; the data show a plateau. The prediction of a decrease is not supported, since the rate does not fall at 80 mM. The ATP-pumping prediction is wrong because no ATP is supplied and facilitated diffusion is passive, moving glucose down its gradient. The company should instead recommend adding more carriers per liposome if faster uptake is needed.

s3-bio-09.stem: An athlete's endurance training doubles the number of GLUT4 glucose transporters in the muscle cell membranes. Based on the data for cells with normal transporter numbers, which prediction best describes glucose uptake in the trained muscle cells?

stimulus.description: Table of glucose uptake rate into cultured muscle cells at five external glucose concentrations.

data.title: Glucose uptake by cultured muscle cells with normal numbers of membrane glucose transporters (GLUT4)
columns: Uptake rate (pmol per cell per min)
data.notes: Cells were incubated with an ATP synthesis inhibitor; uptake rates were unchanged. Glucose concentration inside cells was kept near 0 mM.

options.text: Uptake will be unchanged at all concentrations, because facilitated diffusion depends only on the concentration gradient.
options.why: Misconception: facilitated diffusion is controlled only by the gradient, ignoring that the number of transport proteins limits the rate.

options.text: Uptake will increase only at low external glucose, because the plateau is set by the concentration gradient and will remain near 40.
options.why: Misconception: the plateau is caused by the gradient limit rather than by transporter saturation; the gradient keeps increasing while the rate stays flat, so the gradient is not limiting.

options.text: Uptake will increase at both low and high external glucose, but ATP will now be required to power the additional transporters.
options.why: Misconception: more membrane proteins imply active transport; the data show uptake is independent of ATP, and the process remains passive.

options.text: Uptake will increase at both low and high external glucose, with a plateau near 80 pmol per cell per min, and will still not require ATP.
options.why: Correct: the plateau reflects saturation of transporters, so doubling transporters doubles the maximum rate; unsaturated rates also rise; the process is passive, as the ATP inhibitor data show.

s3-bio-09.explanation_en: Uptake levels off near 40 pmol per cell per min even as external glucose keeps rising, which shows the rate is limited by the number of transporters (saturation), not by the gradient. Doubling transporters therefore raises the maximum rate to about 80 and also raises uptake at low concentrations, where more transporters means more binding and transport events. The ATP inhibitor did not change uptake, so the process is passive and stays so. The prediction that the plateau stays near 40 is wrong because the plateau is not set by the gradient, which keeps increasing while the rate stays flat. The prediction that ATP is now required is wrong because adding more of the same passive transporter does not change its energy needs. The prediction of no change is wrong because transporter number limits the rate.

s3-bio-10.stem: A biotechnology company is deciding whether to spend money converting Strain M, which has both pathway enzymes inside mitochondria, into Strain C, which would have both enzymes free in the cytosol. Using the information in the table, which prediction about Strain C is best supported?

stimulus.description: Table comparing two engineered yeast strains that make the same product through a two-step pathway (enzyme A then enzyme B), differing only in where the enzymes are located.

data.title: Strain comparison for a two-step biosynthetic pathway
columns: Location of enzymes A and B
Intermediate X made per cell per minute (amol)
Product yield (g per liter of culture)
data.notes: Enzyme B has a Km of 150 uM for intermediate X and is not saturated in either strain. Intermediate X does not leave the compartment in which it is made, and the two strains have identical enzyme amounts and activity per molecule. 1 amol = 10^-18 mol; 1 fL = 10^-15 L.

options.text: Product yield will rise, because the cytosol is larger and can hold more enzyme A and enzyme B molecules, so more intermediate X is made per cell.
options.why: Misconception: a larger compartment means more enzyme or more production; the table states enzyme amounts are identical and X production is the same 600 amol/min.

options.text: Product yield will fall, because the same amount of intermediate X is spread through a larger volume, lowering its concentration and the rate of the enzyme B reaction.
options.why: Correct: compartmentalization concentrates substrate in a small volume; in the 20-fold larger cytosolic volume, X concentration is about 20-fold lower, and since enzyme B is unsaturated its rate drops roughly proportionally.

options.text: Product yield will stay the same, because both strains make the same amount of intermediate X per minute, so the total product must be the same.
options.why: Misconception: ignores that reaction rate depends on substrate concentration, not just amount; assumes total amount alone determines output.

options.text: Product yield will fall, because enzymes in the cytosol cannot be active unless they are enclosed by a membrane-bound organelle.
options.why: Misconception: believes enzymes require a membrane-bound organelle to function; cytosolic enzymes work fine, the effect here is concentration and not loss of activity.

s3-bio-10.explanation_en: Compartmentalization keeps substrates and enzymes together in a small volume, which raises the local concentration of intermediate X. Both strains make the same amount of X per minute, but the cytosolic volume (40 fL) is 20 times larger than the mitochondrial volume (2 fL), so X is about 20 times more dilute in Strain C. Because enzyme B is not saturated (substrate well below Km), its rate is roughly proportional to the substrate concentration, so the second step slows and yield falls. The prediction that more enzyme fits in the cytosol is wrong because the enzyme amounts are stated to be identical. The prediction of equal yield is wrong because the rate depends on concentration, not only on the amount made. The prediction that cytosolic enzymes cannot function is wrong because enzymes work in the cytosol; the loss comes from dilution, not inactivity.

s3-bio-11.stem: A researcher measures the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at several substrate concentrations, with and without inhibitor X, as shown in the table. Which statement best explains the effect of inhibitor X on the enzyme?

stimulus.description: Table of initial reaction rate of an enzyme at six substrate concentrations, with and without inhibitor X.

data.title: Initial rate of enzyme-catalyzed reaction (enzyme concentration, pH, and temperature held constant)

options.text: Inhibitor X denatures the enzyme permanently, so the rate is lower at every substrate concentration tested.
options.why: Misconception: equates any reduced rate with denaturation; denaturation would not be overcome by adding substrate, and the rates nearly match at high substrate.

options.text: Inhibitor X binds away from the active site and changes its shape, so it lowers the maximum rate at any substrate level.
options.why: Misconception: confuses competitive with noncompetitive inhibition; a noncompetitive inhibitor would lower the maximum rate even at saturating substrate, but here rates converge (93.0 vs 97.6).

options.text: Inhibitor X binds the active site and competes with substrate, so a high substrate concentration reduces its effect.
options.why: Correct: the rate gap shrinks as substrate rises and the rates converge near the same maximum, the signature of competition for the active site.

options.text: Inhibitor X lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so the reaction proceeds more slowly at low substrate concentration.
options.why: Misconception: reverses the role of activation energy; lowering it would speed the reaction, not slow it, and an inhibitor does not act as a catalyst.

s3-bio-11.explanation_en: Without inhibitor X, the rate at 200 mM substrate is 97.6, and with X it is 93.0. The inhibition is strong at low substrate (6.3 vs 16.7 at 1 mM) but nearly disappears at high substrate. This pattern fits an inhibitor that competes with substrate for the active site: more substrate makes it likelier that substrate occupies the active site, so the maximum rate is almost reached. An inhibitor binding away from the active site would lower the maximum rate even at saturating substrate, and the data do not show that. Denaturation would not be reversed by adding substrate, so it does not fit. Lowering activation energy would speed the reaction rather than slow it, and that is the role of the enzyme, not of an inhibitor.

s3-bio-12.stem: A sports-medicine team tests an experimental drug that slows an enzyme in muscle cells. The enzyme converts pyruvate (the substrate) to lactate. The table shows reaction rates with and without the drug at two substrate concentrations, with the same amount of enzyme in every trial. Which explanation best accounts for the data?

stimulus.description: Table of reaction rate of a muscle enzyme at two substrate concentrations, with and without an inhibitor drug.

data.title: Rate of pyruvate-to-lactate conversion by a muscle enzyme (arbitrary rate units per minute) at 37 degrees C, pH 7.4, fixed enzyme amount

options.text: The drug competes with pyruvate for the active site, so a high pyruvate concentration outcompetes the drug and the rate nearly recovers.
options.why: Correct: inhibition is strong at low substrate (11 vs 33) but almost gone at high substrate (83 vs 95), as expected when inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site.

options.text: The drug permanently denatures some enzyme molecules, so the rate with the drug stays lower by the same proportion at every substrate level.
options.why: Misconception: confuses reversible inhibition with loss of active enzyme; denaturation would reduce the rate by a constant fraction (the data show 33% of normal at 1 mM vs 87% at 40 mM).

options.text: The drug binds to a site away from the active site and changes its shape, so extra pyruvate cannot restore the maximum rate.
options.why: Misconception: describes noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibition and assumes all inhibitors lower maximum rate; here the rate at high substrate is close to the uninhibited rate.

options.text: The drug lowers the activation energy of the reaction more than the enzyme does, so the rate rises at high pyruvate concentration.
options.why: Misconception: thinks an inhibitor acts as a better catalyst; the drug lowers the rate at both concentrations, so it does not speed the reaction.

s3-bio-12.explanation_en: The drug reduces the rate strongly at 1 mM pyruvate (11 vs 33, about 33% of normal) but only slightly at 40 mM (83 vs 95, about 87% of normal). Inhibition that is overcome by more substrate fits competitive inhibition: the drug and pyruvate compete for the same active site, so a high pyruvate concentration makes the active site more likely to be occupied by substrate. The denaturation explanation is wrong because lost enzyme would reduce the rate by the same proportion at every substrate concentration, and the observed proportion changes. The allosteric explanation is wrong because that kind of inhibitor would keep the maximum rate low even with excess substrate, but the rate nearly recovers. The better-catalyst explanation is wrong because the drug lowers the rate at both concentrations, so it is not speeding the reaction or lowering activation energy beyond the enzyme.

s3-bio-13.stem: A researcher prepares a new sample of the same protease, holds it 30 min at pH 12, and then adjusts it to pH 8 for assay. Based on the data, which prediction and reason is best supported?

stimulus.description: Table of initial reaction rate of a bacterial protease measured at different pH values, and rate at pH 8 after 30-min pre-exposure to pH 10 or pH 12.

data.title: Protease activity (all assays at 50 C, saturating substrate)
rows: Held 30 min at pH 10, then assayed at pH 8
Held 30 min at pH 12, then assayed at pH 8

options.text: The rate will rise above 100 umol/min because the enzyme was activated by the stress of the high pH exposure.
options.why: Misconception: stress or extreme conditions activate enzymes; the data show loss of activity, not enhancement.

options.text: The rate will return to about 100 umol/min because changing pH only changes charges temporarily and the shape always recovers.
options.why: Misconception: pH effects are always reversible; the pH 10 data show recovery but the pH 12 data do not, so generalizing is wrong.

options.text: The rate will be about 50 umol/min because half of the enzyme molecules were broken down into amino acids at pH 12.
options.why: Misconception: denaturation is hydrolysis of the enzyme into amino acids; no data support a 50 percent value and denaturation does not break peptide bonds.

options.text: The rate will stay near 4 umol/min because exposure to pH 12 irreversibly altered the enzyme's three-dimensional shape.
options.why: Correct: the pH 12 pre-exposure sample stays at 4 at pH 8, unlike the pH 10 sample that recovered to 98, so denaturation at pH 12 was irreversible.

s3-bio-13.explanation_en: The sample held at pH 12 and then assayed at pH 8 gave only 4 umol/min, almost the same as the rate at pH 12, whereas the sample held at pH 10 recovered to 98. So pH 12 caused irreversible loss of the active-site shape (denaturation), and a new sample treated the same way is predicted to stay near 4. Full recovery to 100 is wrong because the data show recovery only after pH 10, not pH 12. A rate near 50 from peptide breakdown is wrong because denaturation disrupts folding, not peptide bonds, and the data give no support for 50. A rate above 100 is wrong because no data show activation; the enzyme lost activity.

s3-bio-14.stem: A family currently washes protein-stained clothes at 40 °C with a detergent containing the protease described in the table. To save time, they plan to switch to a 60 °C wash with the same detergent, same pH, and same wash duration. Which prediction about enzyme-driven stain removal at 60 °C is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Relative activity of a protease in a laundry detergent measured at pH 9 at five wash temperatures, with a constant substrate amount and a 10-minute reaction time.

data.title: Protease relative activity at pH 9 (10-minute assay, same enzyme and substrate amounts in every trial)
columns: Relative protease activity (% of maximum observed)
data.note: The household currently washes at 40 °C and is considering 60 °C to remove grass and egg stains (protein-based).

options.text: Enzyme-driven stain removal will stay about the same, because the protease is a catalyst and is not changed or used up in the reaction.
options.why: Misconception: believes that because enzymes are not consumed, their activity cannot be affected by environmental conditions; ignores the data showing activity drops.

options.text: Enzyme-driven stain removal will increase, because higher temperature raises the kinetic energy of molecules, so enzyme-substrate collisions become more frequent.
options.why: Misconception: assumes the rate always rises with temperature (collision theory only), ignoring denaturation; contradicts the table showing activity of 20 at 60 °C.

options.text: Enzyme-driven stain removal will decrease, because the high temperature likely disrupts the protease's tertiary structure and active site, so fewer substrate molecules are converted.
options.why: Correct: activity falls from 100 to 20 between 40 and 60 °C, consistent with heat-induced denaturation of the enzyme's tertiary structure and active site.

options.text: Enzyme-driven stain removal will decrease, because the higher temperature lowers the activation energy barrier, so the stain proteins are consumed faster.
options.why: Reaches the right direction with a wrong mechanism: temperature does not lower activation energy (enzymes do), and faster consumption contradicts the decrease in activity.

s3-bio-14.explanation_en: The table shows activity peaking at 40 °C (100%) and dropping to 20% at 60 °C, so enzyme-driven stain removal should fall. The best explanation is that high temperature disrupts the bonds maintaining the protease's tertiary structure, distorting the active site so fewer substrates are converted. The prediction that removal will increase because of more collisions ignores denaturation and contradicts the 60 °C datum. The prediction that nothing changes confuses the fact that catalysts are not consumed with being unaffected by conditions; the data show a clear change. The prediction that removal decreases because heat lowers activation energy gives an incorrect mechanism: enzymes, not temperature, lower activation energy, and a lowered barrier would speed the reaction rather than slow it.

s3-bio-15.stem: DCPIP is a blue dye that accepts electrons and becomes colorless when reduced. A student claims that DCPIP reduction in this experiment depends on the light-dependent reactions carried out by functional chloroplasts. Which choice best supports the claim with evidence from the table?

stimulus.description: Table of DCPIP absorbance at 600 nm before and after 10 minutes for four chloroplast-suspension treatments.

data.title: Absorbance at 600 nm of DCPIP (blue dye; lower absorbance = more DCPIP reduced)
rows: A: Intact chloroplasts + DCPIP, bright light
B: Intact chloroplasts + DCPIP, wrapped in foil (dark)
C: Boiled chloroplasts + DCPIP, bright light
D: Buffer + DCPIP, no chloroplasts, bright light
data.notes: All tubes contained the same buffer, the same DCPIP concentration, and were kept at 25 C. Each value is the mean of three tubes; the range among replicates was within 0.02.

options.text: Absorbance fell by 0.48 in intact chloroplasts in light but by only 0.02 or less in the dark, boiled-chloroplast, and no-chloroplast tubes, so both light and intact chloroplasts were needed.
options.why: Correct: cites the treatment effect (0.48 drop) and the three controls showing that removing light or functional chloroplasts abolishes reduction.

options.text: Absorbance fell by 0.48 in intact chloroplasts in light, which shows that the chloroplasts used light energy to fix carbon dioxide into sugar and thereby reduced the DCPIP.
options.why: Misconception: assumes DCPIP reduction measures carbon fixation/sugar production; the data show only dye reduction, and DCPIP intercepts electrons from the light reactions, not the Calvin cycle.

options.text: Absorbance stayed near 0.80 in the tube with buffer and DCPIP but no chloroplasts in bright light, which shows that light is not required for DCPIP reduction.
options.why: Misconception: misreads the no-chloroplast control; it shows chloroplasts are needed, and says nothing about whether light is unnecessary since the dark tube with chloroplasts also showed no reduction.

options.text: Absorbance fell the most in intact chloroplasts in light, which shows that chloroplasts reduce DCPIP only when ATP is being produced by the Calvin cycle.
options.why: Misconception: attributes the electron source to the Calvin cycle producing ATP; the data do not measure ATP and the Calvin cycle does not supply electrons to DCPIP.

s3-bio-15.explanation_en: The intact-chloroplast tube in light lost 0.48 absorbance units (0.80 to 0.32), while the dark tube (0.02 drop), boiled-chloroplast tube (0.01 drop), and no-chloroplast tube (0 drop) barely changed. Together these show that both light and functional (non-denatured) chloroplasts are required, which supports a claim about the light-dependent reactions. The option claiming sugar synthesis is wrong because the experiment measures only dye reduction, not carbon fixation. The option saying light is not required misuses the no-chloroplast control and ignores the dark chloroplast tube. The option invoking ATP from the Calvin cycle is wrong because no ATP was measured and the Calvin cycle is not the source of electrons for DCPIP.

s3-bio-16.stem: A student will graph the respirometer data in the table to compare the rate of cellular respiration at the two temperatures. Which graph construction best represents these data?

stimulus.description: Table of cumulative oxygen consumed (microliters) by germinating seeds measured every 5 minutes in a respirometer at two temperatures.

data.notes: Each value is the mean of several identical respirometers; time is set by the experimenter, temperature is the manipulated factor.

options.text: A bar graph with temperature on the x-axis and the final O2 value (uL) on the y-axis, with no time information shown
options.why: Misconception: collapsing the data to a single endpoint bar; this hides the time course so rate cannot be read as a slope.

options.text: A line graph with time (min) on the x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed (uL) on the y-axis, two labeled lines (25 C and 15 C) with a legend
options.why: Correct: time is the experimenter-set independent variable on x, the measured response on y, and both temperature series are plotted with a legend, so the slopes (rates) can be compared.

options.text: A line graph with cumulative O2 consumed (uL) on the x-axis and time (min) on the y-axis, one line for each temperature
options.why: Misconception: swapping axes so the dependent variable is on the x-axis; this reverses the convention and makes slope equal to the inverse of the rate.

options.text: A pie chart showing the percentage of total O2 consumed at each time point for the 25 C seeds only
options.why: Misconception: using a pie chart for continuous time-series data; it omits the 15 C group and cannot show rate or compare temperatures.

s3-bio-16.explanation_en: The data are a continuous time series for two conditions, and the goal is to compare rates. A line graph with time (independent variable) on the x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed (dependent variable) on the y-axis, with both temperatures plotted and a legend, lets the slope of each line show the respiration rate (about 2.4 uL/min at 25 C versus about 1.2 uL/min at 15 C). The bar graph of final values discards the time course, so rates cannot be read. The graph with swapped axes breaks the convention of placing the independent variable on the x-axis and makes slope the inverse of the rate. The pie chart is meant for parts of a whole, is not suited to continuous time-series data, and leaves out the 15 C group, so no comparison is possible.

s3-bio-17.stem: A researcher treats cultured liver cells and muscle cells with hormone X and measures the responses shown in the table. Which statement best explains the data in terms of cell communication?

stimulus.description: Table of cAMP and glycogen phosphorylase responses in two cultured cell types after treatment with hormone X, with or without a membrane-impermeable receptor-blocking antibody.

data.title: Responses of cultured cells 10 minutes after treatment
rows: Hormone X + antibody against receptor R
data.note: Hormone X is a water-soluble peptide. Antibody cannot enter cells. Receptor R is a plasma membrane protein.

options.text: Hormone X binds receptor R on both cell types, but only liver cells produce cAMP because muscle cells have no glycogen phosphorylase gene.
options.why: Misconception: ignores that receptor-binding determines target cell; claims receptor is on both cell types, but the lack of any cAMP change in muscle cells indicates no signal is received, and the gene claim is unsupported by the data.

options.text: Hormone X diffuses through the liver cell membrane and binds a cytoplasmic receptor that directly activates glycogen phosphorylase; muscle cells cannot take up hormone X.
options.why: Misconception: assuming all hormones act on intracellular receptors; ignores that a water-soluble peptide is blocked by an extracellular antibody and that cAMP rises, indicating a second-messenger pathway.

options.text: Hormone X binds receptor R on the liver cell surface, which triggers a cAMP-mediated pathway that activates glycogen phosphorylase; muscle cells likely lack receptor R.
options.why: Correct: the blocking antibody (which cannot enter cells) abolishes both cAMP rise and enzyme activation, showing a surface receptor is needed; cAMP rises before/with enzyme activation, consistent with a second messenger; muscle cells show no response, consistent with lacking the receptor.

options.text: Hormone X is converted by liver cells into cAMP, which then acts as the ligand for receptor R and activates glycogen phosphorylase.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the signal with the second messenger; cAMP is made inside the cell in response to receptor activation, and is not the ligand for receptor R.

s3-bio-17.explanation_en: In liver cells, hormone X raises cAMP and glycogen phosphorylase activity. An antibody that cannot enter cells and blocks receptor R eliminates both responses, so the signal is received at a plasma membrane receptor, which fits a water-soluble peptide. cAMP acts as a second messenger that relays the signal inside the cell, leading to enzyme activation. Muscle cells show no change, consistent with target-cell specificity based on having the receptor. The cytoplasmic-receptor idea is wrong because a peptide hormone is blocked by an extracellular antibody and cAMP rises. The idea that both cell types have the receptor is wrong because muscle cells show no signal transduction, and the missing-gene claim is not supported by the data. The idea that hormone X is converted into cAMP that serves as the ligand is wrong because cAMP is generated inside the cell after receptor activation as a second messenger, not as the ligand for the receptor.

s3-bio-18.stem: A sports physiologist studies how skeletal muscle cells respond to epinephrine released during sprinting. Using the data in the table, which statement best explains how epinephrine causes glycogen breakdown in these cells?

stimulus.description: Table of muscle cell responses to epinephrine under four conditions in an exercise-physiology experiment.

data.title: Glycogen breakdown in cultured skeletal muscle cells (relative glucose-1-phosphate released, arbitrary units)
rows: Epinephrine added to the surrounding medium
Epinephrine + drug that blocks the epinephrine receptor on the cell surface
Epinephrine injected directly into the cytoplasm (receptor not involved)

options.text: Epinephrine is taken up by the cell and broken down, and the glucose it releases is used to begin glycogen breakdown.
options.why: Misconception: a signal molecule acts as a fuel or substrate. Injecting epinephrine into the cytoplasm produced no glycogen breakdown, contradicting this.

options.text: Epinephrine diffuses across the plasma membrane and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen in the cytoplasm.
options.why: Misconception: all signaling molecules enter cells and act directly on targets. Direct cytoplasmic injection gave no response (2), so direct action is not supported.

options.text: Epinephrine binds a receptor protein on the cell surface, which triggers a signal transduction pathway inside the cell that activates glycogen-breaking enzymes.
options.why: Correct: response occurs only when epinephrine is outside and the receptor is available; blocking the receptor or bypassing it abolishes the response, indicating surface receptor binding followed by internal transduction.

options.text: Epinephrine changes the permeability of the plasma membrane, and the resulting loss of ions from the cell causes glycogen breakdown.
options.why: Misconception: signals work only by altering membrane permeability. The data show no ion measurements, and the receptor-block result shows a specific receptor is required.

s3-bio-18.explanation_en: Glycogen breakdown is high only when epinephrine is added outside the cell (40) and falls to baseline when the surface receptor is blocked (3) or when epinephrine is put directly in the cytoplasm (2). This shows epinephrine must bind a specific receptor on the cell surface, which starts a signal transduction pathway that activates the enzymes. The direct-activation option is wrong because cytoplasmic epinephrine had no effect. The option claiming epinephrine is metabolized into glucose is wrong for the same reason, and because a signal's role is informational, not as a substrate. The membrane-permeability option is wrong because the data show no ion changes and the response depends on a specific receptor, not on general membrane disruption.

s3-bio-19.stem: A researcher proposes that Ligand L binds a membrane receptor and activates a pathway in which Kinase A phosphorylates Kinase B, which then leads to reporter gene expression. Which statement best connects the data in the table to this proposed signal transduction pathway?

stimulus.description: Table of relative phosphorylation of Kinase A and Kinase B and relative reporter gene expression in cultured cells under four conditions.

data.title: Responses of cultured cells to Ligand L (values are relative units, wild type with ligand = 100 for reporter)
data.notes: Reporter gene is transcribed only when a transcription factor is activated by the pathway. Each knockout cell line lacks only the named kinase and still has a normal receptor for Ligand L.

options.text: Kinase B acts upstream of Kinase A, because loss of Kinase B abolishes the reporter response, while Kinase A phosphorylation stays high.
options.why: Misconception: reversing pathway order by focusing on which knockout stops the output; both knockouts stop the output, and A-P staying high actually shows A is not dependent on B.

options.text: Kinase A acts upstream of Kinase B, because loss of Kinase A prevents Kinase B phosphorylation, while loss of Kinase B leaves Kinase A phosphorylation intact.
options.why: Correct: in the A knockout, B-P is only 6 (near the 4 baseline), so B needs A; in the B knockout, A-P is 90, so A does not need B. This fits A upstream of B in a sequential cascade.

options.text: Kinases A and B act in separate parallel pathways, because each knockout eliminates the reporter response independently of the other kinase.
options.why: Misconception: concluding that two components that both are required for the output must be parallel; but B phosphorylation depends on A, which indicates a linear sequence.

options.text: Kinase A is not needed for the pathway, because Kinase B phosphorylation is still detectable in the Kinase A knockout cells.
options.why: Misconception: misreading the small residual value of 6 as meaningful signaling; it is at the unstimulated baseline (4), so B is essentially not activated without A.

s3-bio-19.explanation_en: In the Kinase A knockout, Kinase B phosphorylation falls to 6, about the unstimulated baseline of 4, so Kinase B activation depends on Kinase A. In the Kinase B knockout, Kinase A is still strongly phosphorylated (90), so Kinase A activation does not depend on Kinase B. Both knockouts abolish reporter expression, so both kinases are required for the response. Together this supports a sequential cascade with Kinase A upstream of Kinase B, as proposed. The option reversing the order is wrong because Kinase A stays phosphorylated without Kinase B, and the loss of the reporter response alone does not indicate order. The parallel-pathway option is wrong because Kinase B phosphorylation depends on Kinase A, so they are not independent. The option claiming Kinase A is unnecessary is wrong because the value of 6 is essentially baseline, not activation, and the reporter response is lost in those cells.

s3-bio-20.stem: An orchard owner wants a spray that prevents premature fruit drop, which is triggered when a hormone activates the pathway described in the table. Before choosing between Inhibitor X and Inhibitor Y, the owner reviews the cell-culture results. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Gene expression in cultured fruit-stalk cells under hormone and treatment conditions, given as percent of the maximum response.

data.title: Expression of fruit-drop gene (% of maximum) in cultured stalk cells
rows: Hormone + Inhibitor X + compound that directly activates kinase B
Hormone + Inhibitor Y + compound that directly activates kinase B
data.pathway_background: Hormone binds a cell-surface receptor -> receptor activates kinase A -> kinase A phosphorylates and activates kinase B -> kinase B activates a transcription factor -> fruit-drop gene is expressed.
data.units: percent of maximum, single mean value per treatment

options.text: Inhibitor X prevents the hormone from entering the cells, because the hormone must enter to activate the kinases.
options.why: Misconception: assumes signaling molecules must enter the cell; the pathway starts with a cell-surface receptor, and the data cannot distinguish hormone entry from other upstream steps.

options.text: Inhibitor X damages the transcription factor, because expression stays low when the hormone and X are present together.
options.why: Misconception: low expression under X alone is taken as proof of a downstream target; ignores the rescue result showing the transcription factor still functions.

options.text: Inhibitor Y is the better choice for the orchard, because it leaves the hormone pathway fully functional in the cells.
options.why: Misconception: reads the goal backward; Y does not reduce expression (96%), so it would not prevent fruit drop, and the pathway being intact is the problem, not a benefit.

options.text: Inhibitor X blocks the pathway at a step before kinase B is activated, because direct activation of kinase B restores expression.
options.why: Correct: expression falls with hormone plus X (8%) but returns to 92% when kinase B is activated directly, so the components from kinase B downstream still work and X acts upstream of kinase B.

s3-bio-20.explanation_en: With hormone plus Inhibitor X, expression drops to 8%, so X interferes with the pathway. When kinase B is activated directly in the presence of X, expression returns to 92%. This shows kinase B, the transcription factor, and the gene are all still functional, so X must act at a step before kinase B is activated (the receptor or kinase A). The claim that X damages the transcription factor is wrong because the transcription factor works when kinase B is activated directly. Inhibitor Y is not a better choice, because it leaves expression at 96% and would not prevent fruit drop. The claim that X blocks hormone entry is unsupported: the receptor is on the cell surface, and the data cannot tell which upstream step X blocks.

s3-bio-21.stem: A hypothetical pathway passes a signal from a receptor to kinase A, then kinase B, then kinase C, which produces the cellular response. The table shows the number of active molecules at each tier produced from one ligand-bound receptor in wild-type and mutant cells. Which claim about the mutant is best supported by the data and by the theory that each active enzyme in a cascade can activate many downstream molecules?

stimulus.description: Table of active molecules at each tier of a hypothetical four-tier signaling cascade, per one ligand-bound receptor, for wild-type and mutant cells.

data.note: Each row gives the number of active molecules at that tier produced from one ligand-bound receptor, measured at steady state.

options.text: The mutation eliminates amplification throughout the cascade, because the mutant shows fewer active molecules than wild type at the final tier.
options.why: Misconception: equating reduced output with total loss of amplification; the receptor to A and B to C steps still amplify tenfold, so only one step is defective.

options.text: The mutation impairs the step in which active kinase B activates kinase C, because kinase C has the fewest active molecules of any tier in the mutant.
options.why: Misconception: assuming the defect lies where the final output is measured; the B to C ratio is 100/10 = 10, identical to wild type, and C is lower only because B is already low.

options.text: The mutation impairs the step in which the ligand-bound receptor activates kinase A, because the mutant response is lower than in wild type.
options.why: Misconception: attributing any reduced response to the first step; kinase A count (10) equals wild type, so receptor activation of A is normal.

options.text: The mutation impairs the step in which active kinase A activates kinase B, because each active kinase A yields one active kinase B in the mutant but ten in wild type.
options.why: Correct: the per-step ratio at A to B falls from 10 to 1, while receptor to A (10) and B to C (10) are unchanged, so the first abnormal step is A to B.

s3-bio-21.explanation_en: Compare the per-step amplification (active molecules at a tier divided by the previous tier). Wild type: 10, 10, 10. Mutant: receptor to A is 10, A to B is 10/10 = 1, and B to C is 100/10 = 10. Only the step from kinase A to kinase B differs, so that step is the one impaired; the low kinase C count is a downstream consequence of the low kinase B count. The claim that the step from B to C is impaired is wrong because that step still amplifies tenfold. The claim about the receptor to A step is wrong because kinase A matches wild type. The claim that amplification is eliminated throughout is wrong because two of the three steps still amplify tenfold.

s3-bio-22.stem: A researcher proposes that hormone H binds a receptor, which leads to cAMP production, and that two kinases (K1 and K2) are in the pathway leading to glucose release. Which argument best uses the data to support a placement of K1 and K2 relative to cAMP?

stimulus.description: Glucose release by cultured liver cells under six treatments.

data.title: Glucose release by cultured liver cells (relative units, mean of 3 trials)
data.note: Pathway components tested: receptor for H, kinase K1, cAMP, kinase K2. Drug X and Drug Y each specifically inhibit only their one target kinase.

options.text: K1 acts upstream of cAMP and K2 acts downstream of cAMP, because the cAMP analog restored glucose release when K1 was inhibited but not when K2 was inhibited.
options.why: Correct: rescue by cAMP analog despite K1 inhibition means K1 is needed only for making cAMP (upstream); failure of rescue with K2 inhibited means K2 is needed after cAMP (downstream).

options.text: K2 acts upstream of cAMP and K1 acts downstream of cAMP, because the cAMP analog restored glucose release when K1 was inhibited but not when K2 was inhibited.
options.why: Reverses the logic of the rescue experiment: the step that can be bypassed by adding the downstream signal is the upstream one.

options.text: K1 and K2 both act downstream of cAMP, because glucose release was low whenever either drug was present with hormone H.
options.why: Uses only the hormone-plus-drug results and ignores the analog rescue in treatment 5; low output with each drug does not show order.

options.text: K1 and K2 both act upstream of cAMP, because glucose release was low whenever either drug was present with hormone H.
options.why: Same error of ignoring the rescue data; also contradicts treatment 6, where K2 inhibition blocks output even when cAMP is supplied.

s3-bio-22.explanation_en: Adding a cAMP analog bypasses any step upstream of cAMP. With Drug X, glucose release returned to near the hormone-only level (95 vs. 100), so K1 is needed only to produce cAMP and acts upstream of it. With Drug Y, the analog did not restore release (13), so K2 is required after cAMP and acts downstream. The reversed-placement option swaps the logic of the rescue. The two options placing both kinases on the same side of cAMP rely only on the inhibited-without-analog results, which show that each kinase is required but not their order, and they contradict the rescue result for K1 (both upstream) or the failure of rescue for K2 (both downstream).

s3-bio-23.stem: A researcher studies the hormone loop described in the table. After the receptor-blocking drug has been given for several days, which prediction about plasma TSH and T4 in the treated rats is best supported by how this feedback loop normally works?

stimulus.description: Mean hormone concentrations in untreated lab rats and the same measures when pituitary receptors for thyroxine (T4) are blocked.

rows: Rats given a drug that blocks T4 receptors on pituitary cells only (n=12)
data.background: In rats, the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release T4. In untreated rats, high plasma T4 reduces TSH release by the pituitary. The thyroid gland and its response to TSH are unaffected by the drug.

options.text: TSH will be higher than in controls and T4 will be higher than in controls, because the pituitary can no longer reduce TSH release in response to T4.
options.why: Correct: negative feedback is lost at the pituitary, so TSH is not suppressed, the thyroid is overstimulated, and T4 rises.

options.text: TSH will be lower than in controls and T4 will be higher than in controls, because the blocked receptors cause the pituitary to release less TSH.
options.why: Misconception: thinking that blocking a receptor for an inhibitory signal reduces output of the target cell (confuses loss of inhibition with loss of stimulation).

options.text: TSH will be higher than in controls and T4 will be lower than in controls, because the blocked receptors prevent T4 from acting on the thyroid.
options.why: Misconception: assuming the drug acts on the thyroid, ignoring that the stem states the block is on pituitary cells only, and breaking the causal chain between TSH and T4.

options.text: TSH and T4 will both stay at control levels, because the thyroid gland still responds normally to TSH and so keeps the system at its set point.
options.why: Misconception: assuming homeostasis is automatically maintained even when the feedback sensor is disabled; ignores that the set point depends on the feedback loop.

s3-bio-23.explanation_en: In the normal loop, T4 acts on the pituitary to lower TSH release (negative feedback). Blocking pituitary T4 receptors removes that inhibition, so TSH rises above 1.0 mU/L. Because the thyroid still responds to TSH, the elevated TSH drives more T4 secretion, so T4 rises above 60 nmol/L, and the loop cannot restore the set point. The prediction that TSH falls while T4 rises is wrong because blocking an inhibitory signal increases, not decreases, pituitary output. The prediction that T4 falls is wrong because the thyroid is unaffected and receives more TSH, not less. The prediction that both stay at control levels is wrong because the set point is maintained by the feedback itself; with the sensor blocked, nothing limits TSH.

s3-bio-24.stem: A researcher analyzes the data from a diploid (2n = 8) testis sample. Population R and population P both have 2C DNA content per cell, yet R cells are considered to have completed the stage of meiosis that reduces chromosome number. Which statement best explains why R cells have 2C DNA but are genetically different from P cells?

stimulus.description: Flow cytometry of cells from a diploid (2n = 8) testis sample sorted by relative DNA content per cell, with the cell stage identified for each group.

columns: Relative DNA content per cell (C units)
rows: Spermatogonia in G1 of the cell cycle
Primary spermatocytes after S phase, before division
Secondary spermatocytes, completed one division after Q
Round spermatids, completed a second division after R
data.unit_note: C = DNA content of one haploid set of unreplicated chromosomes

options.text: DNA replication occurred a second time before the first division, so each R cell has 4 chromosomes with twice the DNA of a haploid cell.
options.why: Misconception: believes DNA is replicated again between divisions; in fact there is no second S phase, and a second replication would not lower DNA from 4C to 2C.

options.text: Sister chromatids separated during the first division, so each R cell has 8 unreplicated chromosomes with one copy of each gene.
options.why: Misconception: confuses meiosis I with mitosis/meiosis II by claiming sister chromatids separate in the first division; this would give 8 unreplicated chromosomes and would not reduce chromosome number.

options.text: Homologous chromosomes separated during the first division, so each R cell has 4 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids.
options.why: Correct: meiosis I separates homologs, halving chromosome number (8 to 4) while each chromosome retains two chromatids, so DNA is 2C (4 chromosomes x 2 chromatids = 8 chromatids = 2 haploid-set equivalents of one chromatid-set each).

options.text: Crossing over between sister chromatids halved the DNA, so each R cell has 8 chromosomes that are identical to those in P cells.
options.why: Misconception: thinks crossing over occurs between sister chromatids and removes DNA; crossing over exchanges segments between nonsister chromatids of homologs and does not change DNA amount or make cells identical to P.

s3-bio-24.explanation_en: P cells are diploid with 8 unreplicated chromosomes (2C). After S phase, Q cells have 8 chromosomes of two sister chromatids each (4C). In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes separate, so each R cell has only 4 chromosomes (one from each homologous pair), but each chromosome still has two sister chromatids. The DNA content is therefore 2C even though the chromosome number is halved, and R cells differ from P cells because they have one member of each homologous pair and are not diploid. The option stating sister chromatids separate in the first division is wrong because that happens in meiosis II (the step that produces the 1C population S). The option with a second round of DNA replication is wrong because no S phase occurs between meiosis I and II, and extra replication would increase DNA rather than lower it from 4C. The option with crossing over between sister chromatids is wrong because crossing over occurs between nonsister chromatids of homologs, does not remove DNA, and produces recombinant rather than identical chromosomes.

s3-bio-25.stem: Which statement best explains, at the level of meiosis, why the seedlings differ genetically from one another while the runner plants do not?

stimulus.description: A household gardener's two propagation options for a heterozygous strawberry plant.

data.text: A household gardener grows one diploid (2n = 14) strawberry plant that is heterozygous at many genes. She is deciding how to get new plants for a larger home garden. Option 1: replant runners (stems that grow from the parent by mitotic cell division). Option 2: plant seeds produced by the plant's flowers, which form from gametes made by meiosis and fertilization. She notices that runner plants all look identical to the parent, but seedlings differ from one another in fruit size and leaf shape.

options.text: During meiosis II, sister chromatids undergo crossing over and are separated at random, so each gamete receives a different combination of alleles.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the stages; crossing over occurs between homologs in meiosis I, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids, which are identical except for rare crossover regions.

options.text: During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes undergo crossing over and are oriented randomly at the metaphase plate, so each gamete receives a different combination of alleles.
options.why: Correct: crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment of homologs in metaphase I generate genetically distinct haploid gametes from a heterozygous parent.

options.text: During meiosis, DNA replication occurs twice with only one division, so each gamete receives a different number of chromosomes.
options.why: Misconception: reverses the pattern; DNA replicates once and cells divide twice, and gametes of this plant each get a haploid set of 7 chromosomes, not varying numbers.

options.text: During meiosis, mutations occur in every gene at a high rate, so each gamete receives different alleles from those of the parent.
options.why: Misconception: attributes variation mainly to mutation; mutations are rare and random, and the main source of variation among gametes is recombination and independent assortment.

s3-bio-25.explanation_en: Meiosis I pairs homologous chromosomes, where crossing over exchanges alleles between non-sister chromatids, and the homologous pairs orient randomly at the metaphase plate, so alleles on different chromosomes assort independently. A heterozygous parent therefore makes many genetically different gametes, and fertilization combines them further, so seedlings differ. Runners form by mitosis, which copies chromosomes and separates sister chromatids to make genetically identical cells. The option about crossing over in meiosis II is wrong because crossing over occurs between homologs in meiosis I, and meiosis II only separates sister chromatids. The option about two replications and one division is wrong because DNA replicates once and the cell divides twice, giving haploid gametes with a consistent chromosome number. The option about frequent mutations is wrong because mutation is rare and is not the main source of the variation produced by meiosis.

s3-bio-26.stem: A sports-medicine clinic reviews the table for a family in which the child has trisomy 21. The extra chromosome 21 came from the mother, whose egg cell was produced by meiosis. Which statement best explains the error in meiosis that produced this egg cell?

stimulus.description: Genetic marker results for a mother and her child with trisomy 21, using a DNA marker located very close to the centromere of chromosome 21.

data.title: Centromere-linked marker on chromosome 21 (alleles named M1 and M2)
data.note: Marker is so close to the centromere that crossing over between the marker and the centromere is negligible. The father contributed one M1 allele; the extra chromosome 21 came from the mother.

options.text: Homologous chromosomes 21 failed to separate in meiosis I, so the egg received both the M1 and M2 homologs.
options.why: Correct: the child received M1 from the father, so the maternal contribution was M1 and M2, two different homologs. With negligible crossing over near the centromere, that happens only if homologs stayed together at anaphase I.

options.text: Sister chromatids of chromosome 21 failed to separate in meiosis II, so the egg received two copies of the same homolog.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the stage of nondisjunction. Failed separation of sister chromatids in meiosis II would give an egg with two identical copies (M1,M1 or M2,M2), not two different alleles.

options.text: Chromosome 21 was replicated twice during the S phase before meiosis I, so the egg received two identical copies of one allele.
options.why: Misconception: believes extra chromosomes come from extra DNA replication. DNA replicates once before meiosis I, and double replication would also not yield two different alleles.

options.text: Homologous chromosomes 21 failed to pair during prophase I, so independent assortment gave the egg an extra copy of the M2 homolog.
options.why: Misconception: thinks failure to pair and independent assortment explains trisomy; independent assortment distributes whole homologs randomly but does not by itself create a gamete with an extra copy, and the data point to separation failure.

s3-bio-26.explanation_en: The father gave one M1 allele, so the mother's egg carried M1 and M2, two different homologs of chromosome 21. Because the marker is next to the centromere and crossing over is negligible, sister chromatids carry identical alleles. Receiving two different alleles therefore means the homologs went to the same pole, which is nondisjunction in meiosis I. Failure of sister chromatids to separate in meiosis II would give two identical alleles, which the data do not show. Extra DNA replication before meiosis I is not the mechanism of trisomy and would not give two different alleles. Failure to pair or independent assortment does not explain an egg that keeps both homologs, since the chromosomes would still be distributed one per pole if separation worked.

s3-bio-27.stem: A student tests the null hypothesis that the two genes assort independently, with purple (P) and smooth (S) completely dominant, using the F2 data in the table. Which conclusion is best supported by a chi-square test at p = 0.05?

stimulus.description: F2 kernel phenotype counts from a maize dihybrid cross, with chi-square critical values.

data.title: F2 kernels from a cross of two heterozygous (PpSs x PpSs) maize plants
data.null_hypothesis: Alleles of the two genes assort independently with complete dominance (9:3:3:1)

options.text: Chi-square is about 330 with 3 degrees of freedom, above 7.81, so the null hypothesis is rejected.
options.why: Misconception: using equal 1:1:1:1 expected counts (135 each) instead of 9:3:3:1, which gives a large chi-square.

options.text: Chi-square is about 1.0 with 3 degrees of freedom, but the observed counts differ from the expected counts, so the null hypothesis is rejected.
options.why: Misconception: any difference between observed and expected counts means rejection, ignoring comparison with the critical value.

options.text: Chi-square is about 1.0 with 4 degrees of freedom, below 9.49, so the null hypothesis is proven true.
options.why: Misconception: df equals the number of categories, and failing to reject proves the null true.

options.text: Chi-square is about 1.0 with 3 degrees of freedom, below 7.81, so the null hypothesis is not rejected.
options.why: Correct: expected 303.75, 101.25, 101.25, 33.75 give chi-square about 1.0; df = 4 categories - 1 = 3; 1.0 < 7.81 so fail to reject.

s3-bio-27.explanation_en: Expected counts under 9:3:3:1 for 540 kernels are 303.75, 101.25, 101.25 and 33.75. The chi-square sum of (O-E)^2/E is about 1.0. With 4 phenotype classes, df = 3 and the critical value is 7.81. Since 1.0 is below 7.81, the null hypothesis is not rejected; the deviations are consistent with chance. The option rejecting because counts differ ignores that small deviations are expected by chance. The option using 4 degrees of freedom miscounts df, and a test can never prove the null true, only fail to reject it. The option with a chi-square near 330 uses the wrong expected ratio (equal classes) rather than the ratio predicted by independent assortment.

s3-bio-28.stem: Using the data in the table, a student tests the null hypothesis that the offspring follow a 9:3:3:1 ratio, using a significance level of p = 0.05. Which result and conclusion are correct?

stimulus.description: Observed counts of four phenotype classes among 640 offspring from a cross of two individuals heterozygous at two unlinked genes, with a hypothesized 9:3:3:1 ratio.

options.text: χ² ≈ 5.6 with 3 degrees of freedom; this is below 7.81, so the null hypothesis is not rejected.
options.why: Misconception: computing with ratio proportions or counts incorrectly (e.g., dividing by observed or omitting squares), producing a small value and concluding the counts look close enough.

options.text: χ² ≈ 17.8 with 3 degrees of freedom; this exceeds 7.81, so the null hypothesis is supported.
options.why: Misreads the decision rule: a value above the critical value means rejection, not support.

options.text: χ² ≈ 17.8 with 3 degrees of freedom; this exceeds 7.81, so the null hypothesis is rejected.
options.why: Correct: expected 360,120,120,40 give χ²=17.8, df=3, above 7.81, so reject.

options.text: χ² ≈ 17.8 with 4 degrees of freedom; this is below 18.5, so the null hypothesis is not rejected.
options.why: Misconception: using number of classes as df instead of classes minus 1, and then using an unrelated critical value to reach a wrong decision.

s3-bio-28.explanation_en: Expected counts from 9:3:3:1 with n = 640 are 360, 120, 120 and 40. χ² = (340-360)²/360 + (140-120)²/120 + (100-120)²/120 + (60-40)²/40 ≈ 1.11 + 3.33 + 3.33 + 10.0 ≈ 17.8. With four classes, df = 3 and the critical value at p = 0.05 is 7.81. Because 17.8 > 7.81, the null hypothesis is rejected. The option saying the null is supported misreads the rule, since a value above the critical value never supports the null. The option with χ² ≈ 5.6 rests on a miscalculation, and the observed counts are in fact not close enough. The option using 4 degrees of freedom miscounts df, which is the number of classes minus one, and its decision is also wrong.

s3-bio-29.stem: A researcher grows genetically identical cuttings of one plant line in growth chambers under the conditions shown in the table. Which statement best explains the pattern of flower color in the data?

stimulus.description: Table of mean flower color score (0 = white, 10 = deep blue) for genetically identical cuttings of one hydrangea-like plant line grown in growth chambers at three soil pH values and for two chamber temperatures.

data.title: Mean flower color score of cuttings from a single clonal plant line (n = 20 cuttings per condition)
data.notes: All cuttings were taken from one parent plant and are genetically identical. Light, water, and nutrients were identical in all chambers.

options.text: Soil pH influences how the shared genotype is expressed, so phenotype varies with pH even without genetic differences among the plants.
options.why: Correct: identical genotypes with other factors held constant yet color differs strongly across pH, so environment affects phenotype; temperature has little effect.

options.text: Chamber temperature changes the genotype of the cuttings, so plants at 30 C carry different alleles from plants at 20 C.
options.why: Misconception: environment alters the DNA sequence/genotype; also the data show temperature has almost no effect on color.

options.text: Mutations caused by acidic soil produced new flower color alleles in the cuttings grown at pH 4.5.
options.why: Misconception: environmental conditions cause directed mutations that create new alleles; no evidence of mutation, and effect is environmental expression.

options.text: Flower color in this line is determined only by genotype, so the differences among soil pH groups arose from random sampling error.
options.why: Misconception: phenotype depends on genotype alone; ignores that differences across pH (about 8 points) are far larger than within-pH variation between temperatures.

s3-bio-29.explanation_en: All cuttings are clones and light, water and nutrients were constant, so the large drop in color score as pH rises (about 8.6 to 0.85) must come from the environment influencing expression of the same genotype. The option claiming temperature changes the genotype is wrong because genotype is the DNA sequence, which an environmental condition does not rewrite, and temperature barely changed color (differences of 0.2 or less). The option about acidic soil causing new alleles is wrong because nothing in the data shows mutation, and a graded, reversible-type response across pH reflects expression, not new alleles. The option attributing differences to genotype alone and sampling error is wrong because the genotype is the same in all groups and the pH differences are large and consistent compared with the tiny differences between temperatures.

s3-bio-30.stem: A garden center owner wants to sell hydrangeas that bloom pink. She buys cuttings that all came from one parent plant and tests them as shown in the table. Which statement about the cause of the flower-color differences is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Table of flower color and measured aluminum uptake for genetically identical hydrangea clones grown in three soil pH treatments, 10 plants per treatment.

data.title: Clones of one hydrangea cultivar (all cuttings from a single parent plant) grown 12 months in identical pots, light, and watering, differing only in soil pH
columns: Aluminum in sepals (mg per kg dry mass), mean

options.text: Aluminum uptake is the same in every treatment, so soil pH has no effect on the phenotype of these plants.
options.why: Misconception from misreading data: aluminum uptake clearly differs (212, 96, 18), and color differs with pH.

options.text: Soil pH caused mutations in the flower-color genes of the cuttings, producing three different genotypes with three different colors.
options.why: Misconception: environmental factors induce genotype-changing mutations; the data show no DNA change and the color change tracks the environment, not a heritable alteration.

options.text: Flower color is determined entirely by genotype, so the color differences must reflect hidden genetic variation among the cuttings.
options.why: Misconception: phenotype is fixed by genotype alone; cuttings are clones, so genetic differences cannot explain the differences.

options.text: Soil pH changes how much aluminum the plants take up, so the environment influenced how the same genotype was expressed as flower color.
options.why: Correct: identical genotypes plus controlled conditions except pH, with color tracking pH and aluminum uptake, shows an environmental effect on phenotype.

s3-bio-30.explanation_en: The cuttings are clones from one parent, so they share a genotype, and all conditions except soil pH were held constant. Flower color differs systematically with pH and with aluminum uptake (212, 96, 18 mg/kg), so the environment altered the phenotype produced by the same genotype. The mutation option is wrong because nothing in the data indicates DNA changes, and a pH-dependent color shift is a plastic response rather than a new genotype.
